narrative: During the 1940s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in tradition and identity. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth of afro-textured hair, was likely becoming increasingly popular as it would gain widespread recognition and celebration during the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s. Cornrows, a traditional African braiding practice, were also being worn, showcasing the rich cultural heritage of Africa and its diaspora. While there is limited documentation on hairstyles from this era, we can infer that protective styles such as Bantu knots and possibly box braids were being worn to minimize hair manipulation and exposure to environmental elements. These hairstyles not only protected the hair but also became a symbol of resistance against societal norms and expectations. The Jheri curl, invented later in the 1980s, was not yet available during this time period. Unfortunately, due to the scarcity of source material from this era, we can only speculate on the specific hairstyles and trends that defined Black and African women's hair culture in the 1940s.
